title: Why Being Wrong Can Feel So Right
author: Lee LeFever
summary: Lee LeFever continues his Science of Explanation series by showing how mental patterns, which researchers call schemas and scripts, help us grasp new ideas and also lead us astray. He uses Schank and Abelson's restaurant script, and the cafeteria that bends it, to show how existing patterns give us a head start in unfamiliar situations. He then shows the downside with a thermostat: someone used to gas burners turns the dial to maximum expecting faster heating, though a thermostat only sets a target temperature. The mind constantly tries to fit new information into what we already know, so a plausible but wrong explanation can feel correct. For communicators, this means audience assumptions are invisible and tied to the curse of knowledge. His advice is to anticipate the patterns the audience holds, make connections and causal mechanisms visible, and help people update their patterns rather than assume they share yours.
points: A schema is organized knowledge about a familiar situation, and it spares us from understanding every new experience from scratch.
Familiar patterns can mislead: the thermostat example shows a plausible explanation feeling correct while being wrong.
Because patterns feel obvious to the expert, the curse of knowledge makes communicators leave out the very connections the audience needs.
Good explanation asks what patterns the audience likely holds and explicitly shows mechanisms and causal relationships to update them.
quotes: We interpret new information using what we already know. Our existing knowledge and experience help shape what we notice, how we understand it, and what we remember.
A “schema” is organized knowledge about a familiar kind of object, event, or situation, including relationships and expectations.
In this way, patterns give us a head start in adjusting to a new situation.
A key idea to remember: the mind is constantly trying to fit new information into what we already know.
So you turn the thermostat to the maximum setting, expecting it to heat faster. The context and your existing knowledge provided a plausible explanation that felt correct to you.
The problem was not the reality of thermostats, but expectations you brought to the table.

Everyone has patterns and expectations that are invisible. Part of clear communication is anticipating the audience’s assumptions (dials lead to faster heating) and finding ways to update their patterns.
